strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: scalable data valuation for modern LLMs and VLMs, where Hessian-, checkpoint-, and retraining-based methods are often impractical.

For-Value is conceptually simple and easy to deploy: it uses hidden-state similarity and token-level prediction residuals from a single forward pass over the data, without backpropagation, Hessians, or stored training checkpoints.

The proposed score has a clear closed-form interpretation as an inner product between output-layer prediction-error features, and the derivation in Theorem 1 and Appendix 8.2 provides a principled motivation under explicitly stated assumptions.

Empirical results are strong across several LLM and VLM tasks and model families, including models up to 72B parameters. For-Value is usually competitive with or better than Hessian-free, DataInf, HyperINF, and embedding-similarity baselines while being dramatically faster.
The ablation showing the importance of the prediction-error term α, the qualitative rankings, and the explicit runtime/complexity analysis collectively support the practical value of the method.
The appendix gives substantial reproducibility support, including the algorithm, dataset statistics, task templates, training configurations, hyperparameters, and licensing information.
weaknesses: The theory has a substantial gap to the actual deployment setting. The unconstrained-feature assumption treats hidden representations as free or sample-specific quantities, and the derivation is essentially an output-layer gradient inner product with respect to the unembedding matrix W. It does not fully model shared lower-layer parameters, hidden-state drift, or gradients arising in full or LoRA fine-tuning.

Describing the method as entirely ‘gradient-free’ somewhat overstates its novelty: the score can be viewed as reconstructing last-layer gradient similarity without invoking autograd. The relationship to ordinary gradient dot products and to the Emb baseline should be discussed more sharply.

The main evidence is based on proxy labels—same class, style, or task—on highly templated datasets. Near-perfect AUC may therefore reflect how easily pretrained representations separate synthetic task classes rather than true counterfactual influence.

The paper does not directly validate influence through leave-one-out retraining, data addition/removal, or correlation between assigned values and actual changes in validation NLL or downstream performance. Such an experiment, even on a smaller model, would much more directly support the central data-valuation claim.

The evaluation is relatively narrow: synthetic sentence transformation and math tasks, image-captioning subject/style tasks, and one cats-versus-dogs mislabeling benchmark. Results on real-world noisy NLP datasets or more open-ended generation tasks would improve generalization.

Some claimed advantages are small and may not be statistically significant because confidence intervals overlap. For example, on mislabeled detection with the 11B VLM, DataInf achieves AUC 1.000 while For-Value achieves 0.995. Multiple-seed comparisons and significance tests would strengthen the conclusions.

The efficiency comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: some baselines use quantization, some large-model runtimes are extrapolated from 10% of validation data, different numbers of GPUs are used, and baselines are not reported at all sizes such as 72B. The theoretical complexity also largely omits backbone forward-pass costs.

Several evaluation details could be clearer, especially the exact top-k definition used for Recall. I also did not see an explicit code-release commitment, which would strengthen reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: Targets an important practical bottleneck: existing gradient-, Hessian-, and Shapley-based data-valuation methods are difficult to use with billion-parameter LLMs and VLMs. For-Value removes backpropagation, checkpoint tracking, and per-sample gradient storage, enabling large-batch valuation.

The proposed closed-form score is well motivated and easy to implement. It combines alignment of last-layer hidden representations with token-level prediction-error similarity, and the derivation clearly distinguishes it from naive embedding similarity such as Emb.

The algorithm is batch-scalable and uses a sparse, sample- or batch-specific vocabulary to avoid the full vocabulary cost. The paper also provides a useful complexity comparison against influence-function, Hessian-based, DataInf, HyperINF, and embedding methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering LLMs and VLMs, multiple model families, model sizes from 1.5B to 72B parameters, influential-example detection, mislabeled-data detection, and data selection for downstream fine-tuning.

For-Value is consistently competitive with or better than gradient-based baselines on identification tasks, while providing substantial wall-clock speedups. Downstream selection results on GSM8K, noisy medical reasoning, and medical VQA demonstrate practical utility beyond synthetic ranking metrics.

The paper includes ablations on the prediction-error term, performance across model sizes, qualitative examples, implementation details, and a proof in the appendix, supporting reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: The theoretical result relies on strong idealizations: unconstrained features, distinct training and valuation inputs, and a first-order analysis at initialization. It does not directly establish the claim for bounded Transformer representations, frozen or LoRA-tuned unembedding layers, or later stages of multi-step fine-tuning. Additional sensitivity analyses or more qualified claims would strengthen confidence.

The influential-data metrics use class-based pseudo-labels and largely templated tasks, so high AUC and recall can partly reflect class, template, or style similarity rather than causal data value. More evaluations with naturally noisy or mislabeled NLP datasets would improve external validity.

Downstream fine-tuning results are generally promising but sometimes based on small differences and do not report standard deviations or statistical significance. For-Value is also not uniformly best, for example on the 20% PMC-Reasoning setting and a few individual AUC/Recall entries; the empirical-superiority wording should be more nuanced.

Some runtime comparisons are difficult to audit. Large-model For-Value inference uses four GPUs, while several baseline measurements use a single GPU and are extrapolated from a 10% valuation subset. End-to-end runtime, aggregate GPU time, and peak memory should be compared under identical hardware and data settings.

The behavior of the sparse-vocabulary approximation on long, diverse, open-domain outputs and with many valuation samples is not fully characterized empirically. The final submission should also ensure that the promised code, scripts, and exact model/data configurations are publicly and permanently available.
